summary: Gives guidelines for designers using UDP, focusing on congestion control but also covering message size, reliability, checksums and middleboxes. It is a BCP.

eli5.summary: UDP is a fast but careless delivery service. This is a safety guide for using it responsibly.

subtitle: A design checklist for anyone building on UDP, centered on the fact that UDP will not slow down for you when the network is congested.

tldr.problem: UDP has no congestion control, so an application can send at the speed of its link and push a path into congestion, and it also leaves reliability, ordering, message size and middlebox behavior to the application.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC lays out guidelines for UDP users: control the sending rate, keep datagrams below the path MTU, handle loss, duplication and reordering, enable checksums, cope with NATs and firewalls, and protect against spoofed traffic.
tldr.outcome: Most applications are told to follow the guidelines or explain why not, and to prefer an existing IETF transport such as TCP when they can. It obsoletes RFC 5405 and has been updated by RFC 8899.

today: RFC 8085 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 145) published in March 2017. It obsoletes RFC 5405 and has been updated by RFC 8899.

sections.title: Why UDP Needs Guidelines
sections.content:
UDP gives applications a minimal, unreliable, best-effort way to send messages over IP. It sets up no connection, so it has no setup or teardown cost and little state. That makes it efficient for some applications.

The catch is that UDP has no inherent congestion control. On many platforms an application can send datagrams at the line rate of its link, which is often far above what the path can carry. RFC 2914 names two reasons congestion control matters: preventing congestion collapse (more load producing less useful work) and establishing some fairness between flows. Even slow senders matter: five 1500-byte datagrams in one second can already exceed a 56 Kb/s path.

This document is a Best Current Practice, not a protocol. Applications are expected to follow it, and where they have good reason not to, they are RECOMMENDED to cite the relevant section and explain their rationale. It obsoletes RFC 5405 and adds guidance for multicast, anycast, broadcast and tunnels.
sections.eli5: UDP is like a person who can shout as loudly as they like in a crowded room. This guide tells them how to be polite so everyone can still talk.

sections.title: Congestion Control for UDP
sections.content:
Applications MUST NOT assume anything about a path's delay, bandwidth, loss or message size, and instead must work safely under varied conditions. The simplest route is usually an existing IETF transport such as TCP, SCTP or DCCP. Applications that choose UDP SHOULD control their sending rate across all the UDP traffic they send to a destination, even if it comes from many sockets or processes.

  • Bulk transfers (more than a few datagrams per round trip) SHOULD use TFRC, window-based TCP-like control, or something that competes fairly with TCP within an order of magnitude.
  • Low data-volume applications SHOULD send on average no more than one datagram per round-trip time. If they cannot estimate RTT, an initial interval of 1 second is recommended, and with no return traffic at all they SHOULD NOT send more than one datagram every 3 seconds.
  • Timers: expiry of a loss-detection timer MUST be treated as a sign of congestion, and latency samples MUST NOT come from ambiguous retransmissions.
  • Bursts: applications SHOULD pace transmissions rather than send long line-rate bursts.
  • Both directions: a request-response application SHOULD control both its requests and its responses.

Congestion control should not be bolted on afterwards. The RFC compares it to security, which has to be considered throughout the design.
sections.eli5: If you send mail faster than the post office can carry it, everything piles up. So you should watch how fast things are getting through and slow down when they are not.

sections.title: ECN, DiffServ, Reserved Capacity and Circuit Breakers
sections.content:
UDP applications can use Explicit Congestion Notification (ECN), but only with a full set of mechanisms: negotiating that the peer can give ECN feedback, checking the ECN field on every received datagram, reporting CE-marked datagrams back to the sender, and reducing the rate at least as much as TCP would. Applications that cannot do this are encouraged to use a transport that already supports ECN.

Applications can set a Differentiated Services Code Point (DSCP), but markings may be changed or removed along the path, so applications SHOULD NOT rely on a specific treatment. Likewise they SHOULD NOT assume QoS is available on the Internet.

Some applications, such as multicast IPTV inside access networks, run over pre-provisioned or reserved capacity and MAY skip congestion control. That is not safe on the wider Internet: leaked traffic can cause congestion collapse. Such applications SHOULD NOT be unadaptive by default and SHOULD deploy a circuit breaker, an automatic mechanism that detects excessive congestion and stops or sharply reduces the flow. Internet applications with no congestion control SHOULD implement one.
sections.eli5: Some roads are reserved just for you, so you can drive fast. But if you drive onto a public road, you need a safety switch that makes you stop when traffic gets bad.

sections.title: Tunnels and Multicast
sections.content:
UDP is often used as a tunnel, wrapping another protocol's packets in UDP datagrams. The RFC splits tunnels into three cases. If the tunnel carries congestion-controlled IP traffic at a matching volume, it SHOULD NOT use its own congestion control, since losses already trigger a response at the original senders; a circuit breaker may help. If the payload is not known to be IP or is not congestion controlled, the tunnel SHOULD use congestion control or a circuit breaker. If the tunnel's UDP volume does not follow the payload volume, it goes beyond these guidelines and the designer SHOULD consider a circuit breaker. Tunnels SHOULD also restrict the types of traffic they carry.

For multicast and broadcast, per-receiver feedback scales badly, so applications SHOULD still provide congestion control that copes with very different receivers. The RFC describes feedback-based and receiver-driven styles, where receivers join or leave multicast groups to change their own rate. A multicast application SHOULD NOT send datagrams larger than the effective MTU.
sections.eli5: A tunnel is a box inside a box. If the inner box already follows the traffic rules, the outer box does not need to add its own.

sections.title: Message Size, Reliability and Checksums
sections.content:
Message size. A UDP datagram is limited to a payload of 65,507 bytes for IPv4 and 65,527 bytes for IPv6, but fragmentation lowers reliability and efficiency, so applications SHOULD NOT send datagrams that exceed the path MTU. They SHOULD use path MTU discovery, or fall back to messages shorter than the default effective MTU for sending: 576 bytes for IPv4 (or the first-hop MTU if smaller) and 1280 bytes for IPv6. To find the payload size, subtract the IP header and the 8-byte UDP header from the PMTU.

Reliability. UDP does not retransmit, suppress duplicates or keep order. Applications that need those MUST provide them, and SHOULD tolerate delayed or duplicate packets within a 2-minute interval, borrowing TCP's Maximum Segment Lifetime. Retransmissions are themselves subject to congestion control.

Checksums. Applications SHOULD enable the UDP checksum. It is weak and does not protect against malicious modification, so data that must stay intact needs extra checks such as a CRC or cryptographic hash. Over IPv6 the checksum MUST be used, except for tunnels that meet the RFC 6935 and RFC 6936 conditions for zero-checksum mode. UDP-Lite can deliver partly damaged payloads for applications that tolerate them, but few middleboxes understand it.
sections.eli5: Big parcels get torn apart on the way, so use small ones. Do not count on every parcel arriving, or arriving once, or arriving in order. And add your own seal if the contents are important.

sections.title: Middleboxes, Keep-alives and Ports
sections.content:
NATs and firewalls keep per-flow state for UDP and delete it after a period of silence, after which replies are dropped. Applications SHOULD handle this gracefully and be able to re-establish their sessions. Some, such as media applications, MAY send keep-alive messages, but these are NOT RECOMMENDED for general use. If used, they SHOULD NOT be sent more often than once every 15 seconds, with slight random jitter. NATs require a state timeout of 2 minutes or longer per RFC 4787, but the RFC notes that many deployed middleboxes use shorter ones.

On ports, a UDP sender SHOULD NOT use source port zero, and applications SHOULD use a randomized source port, or an equivalent check, to resist off-path data injection. Tunnels that use the source port for load-balancing entropy SHOULD pick from the ephemeral range 49152 to 65535 and SHOULD NOT change the port for a flow more than once in thirty seconds. Using many UDP flows in parallel can strain middlebox state, and applications MUST NOT assume consistent middlebox behavior.

Applications SHOULD validate the payload of ICMP errors and SHOULD NOT rely on ICMP being delivered, since middleboxes increasingly filter it.
sections.eli5: The doorman at an office forgets you after a while if you stay quiet. You can wave every so often, but not constantly. And you should use a different random knock each time so strangers cannot guess it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
UDP provides no communications security. Applications that need protection against eavesdropping, tampering or forgery SHOULD use end-to-end security from other IETF protocols. IPsec can secure UDP flows, and DTLS encrypts UDP payloads without needing operating system support, though it does not protect the UDP headers. The RFC RECOMMENDS well-known standard mechanisms such as DTLS or IPsec over inventing new ones.

Applications that answer short requests with large responses can be abused for amplification attacks and SHOULD take steps to limit this, for instance by authenticating the sender (the source address alone is not an authenticator) or limiting how many requests they answer. Long-lived UDP associations ought to periodically check that the receiver still consents to receive traffic. The RFC also notes that some operators limit UDP rates because of attack surges, which can in turn limit what an application achieves over UDP.
sections.eli5: UDP does not lock the envelope. If your message is private, put it in a locked box. And do not let strangers trick you into sending big replies to someone else.

items.title: IP payload, matching volume
items.text: SHOULD NOT add its own congestion control. A circuit breaker may help.

items.title: Non-IP or uncontrolled payload
items.text: SHOULD use congestion control or a circuit breaker.

items.title: Volume unrelated to payload
items.text: Beyond these guidelines. SHOULD consider a circuit breaker.
